A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the rate of cesarean delivery in HIV-infected women has been steadily decreasing in the era of combined antiretrovial therapy (cART) and that the risk of vertical transmission is extremely low in women with undetectable viral loads.
we found that women with HIV who have low viral loads and who are on combination antiretrovirals can safely opt for a vaginal delivery in the presence of an obstetrically favorable pelvis.
women with HIV on ART with low viral loads have a similar risk of vertical transmission whether they deliver vaginally or by cesarean section.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cesarean section is not indicated for HIV-infected pregnant women on antiretrovirals with low viral loads, even in the absence of a viral load test.
women living with HIV who have a low plasma viral load at the time of delivery can have vaginal delivery without an increased risk of vertical transmission.
women with HIV infection on combination antiretrovirals and with viral loads <1000 copies/mL can safely choose vaginal delivery, even without a prior cesarean section.
